title: Context & Memory
description: How agents hold information — and how to manage it

units.title: When the agent didn't get you

objectives.text: Explain that at any moment the agent knows only what is in its “field of view”, and recognize three context problems: lost in the middle, context rot, distractors
Separate context (stable background) from the prompt (the instruction for this request) and split them explicitly with headings or XML tags
Choose where to store information: the project’s CLAUDE.md, the personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, TODO.md, AGENTS.md, and tell them apart from MEMORY.md, which Claude writes itself
Explain why a memory file must be short, and trim a bloated CLAUDE.md
Apply long-session techniques: a summary compression before a new session and parallel agents for independent subtasks

checks.question: According to the lesson, which preparation for a task will give the agent the best result?
options: 3–5 relevant files and a clean prompt for the task
All 200 project files and two hours of history: the more the agent knows, the more reliable it is
Only the chat history, no files: everything has already been said there
All the files, but with the important ones in the middle so the agent reads them more carefully
checks.explain: The agent works with what is in its field of view. Anything extra becomes distractors, and the middle gets lost (u1, “Fix: manage what’s in ‘field of view’”).

checks.question: Two hours into one session, the answers have got worse and invented details have appeared. Which context problem is this?
options: Lost in the middle
Distractors
Context rot
Mixing context and prompt
checks.explain: Hallucinations growing with the length of the conversation are a sign of context rot. Lost in the middle is about where data sits in the context; distractors are about similar extra fragments (u1, “Three context problems”).

checks.question: Request: “I’m a startup founder writing to an investor, style is concise and confident. Write an email.” Where is the prompt here in the lesson’s sense?
options: The whole text is the prompt
“Write an email” is the prompt, the rest is context
“Style is concise and confident” is the prompt, since it’s an instruction on how to write
“I’m a startup founder” is the prompt, the rest is context
checks.explain: The prompt is a specific instruction for this request. Who you are, whom you’re writing to and in what style is information about the world, that is, context (u2, “Separating context and prompt”).

checks.question: How does the lesson suggest laying out context and task in one message?
options: As one paragraph, but with the task as the first sentence
Send the context as one message and the task as the next, with no markers
Repeat the context inside every line of the task
Separate them explicitly: headings “## CONTEXT” and “## TASK” or tags `<context>` and `<task>`
checks.explain: The lesson gives two ways to separate explicitly: Markdown headings and XML tags. The model must see where the stable background is and where the instruction is (u2, “How to separate them explicitly”).

checks.question: The agent needs your personal preferences in every project. Where do you store them?
options: In each project’s CLAUDE.md
In TODO.md
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
Write them at the start of every session
checks.explain: A specific project’s rules and stack are stored in its CLAUDE.md, while personal things common to all projects go in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (u2, “Where to store stable context”).

checks.question: CLAUDE.md has grown to a thousand lines, and the agent has started following the rules worse. What should you do according to the lesson?
options: Add more rules to close the gaps
Move everything to TODO.md
Delete CLAUDE.md and explain everything verbally each time
Trim the file down to the essentials: the longer it is, the worse the agent follows instructions
checks.explain: A memory file’s length works against it. The lesson sets a guideline of about 200 lines, and explaining verbally every time is the opposite extreme (u3, reflection and “Limit”).

checks.question: How is MEMORY.md different from CLAUDE.md, TODO.md and AGENTS.md?
options: Claude writes it itself, it’s stored only locally, and you can view and edit it via `/memory`
It isn’t: it’s just another file you fill in yourself
It lives in the repository and is shared by the whole team
It’s another name for AGENTS.md
checks.explain: You write the lesson’s three files. Claude maintains MEMORY.md itself; it’s local automatic memory (u3, “MEMORY.md — Claude’s auto-memory”).

checks.question: You’re switching from Claude Code to another agent (Aider, Cline). What from the lesson on memory still holds?
options: Nothing: CLAUDE.md is specific to Claude Code
The idea itself: stable context lives in a file, and the agent reads it at session start; only the file names change
Memory transfers between tools automatically
You’ll have to paste the context into every message by hand
checks.explain: CLAUDE.md is one implementation of the “persistent context file” pattern. Other agents have their own files, but the principle is the same (u3, callout “Not just Claude Code”).

checks.question: The agent made a mistake, and you fixed it. According to the lesson’s table, where do you write a rule so the mistake doesn’t happen again?
options: In TODO.md
In AGENTS.md
Nowhere: I’ll fix it again next time
In the “How to run” section of CLAUDE.md
checks.explain: Architecture and stack are updated in CLAUDE.md, completed tasks in TODO.md, and rules for the agent’s behavior after its mistake in AGENTS.md (u4, “When to update what”).

checks.question: The session context has filled up, and the work isn’t finished. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Ask for a brief summary in the format “Done / Left / Issues” and start a new session with it
Keep going in the same chat: the model remembers everything said
Copy the entire chat history into the new session
Start a new session from scratch with nothing carried over
checks.explain: Context compression keeps the essence and doesn’t drag into the new window a long history that is already degrading the answers (u4, “Context compression”; u1, Context Rot).

checks.question: For which tasks does the lesson suggest running several agents in parallel?
options: For steps of one chain, where each depends on the previous one
For one task given to three agents for reliability
For any task: parallel is always faster
For independent subtasks whose results are merged afterwards
checks.explain: In the lesson’s example, three subtasks in different modules don’t depend on each other, so they can run in parallel and then be merged (u4, “Parallel agents for big tasks”).
